open_obligations: Check that 'approximate global equilibrium' in Buhl et al. matches A-leading Stackelberg equilibria.
Check that the safety case accounts for the stability and A-provability conditions.
Note the guarantee is average-case over inputs.

Theorem 6.2 is a formal result about the prover-estimator debate protocol, while claim 2 is about the system in the safety case; check that this system and its debate game fit the theorem's model, not only its equilibrium notion and hypotheses.

Buhl et al. call prover-estimator debate forthcoming and say their argument structure should apply to other protocols; check that claim 2 is meant to rest on this protocol's Theorem 6.2 and not only on some protocol with honest equilibria.
in.other_title: Four key claims of the debate safety case: equilibrium, error bound, no drift, low stakes
in.rationale: Buhl et al.'s key claim 2 is that in approximate global equilibria the system errs on at most an eps'-fraction of cases. They require a debate protocol in whose global equilibrium both debaters are honest, and say they wrote the sketch with prover-estimator debate (forthcoming) in mind, though the argument structure should apply to other protocols. Brown-Cohen et al. state that debaters can be trained in prover-estimator debate via standard methods that converge to Stackelberg equilibria in zero-sum games, and that, given rho-stability and A-provability, Theorem 6.2 implies A will produce the correct answer with probability at least 1 - 5 eps, which is the kind of result claim 2 needs.
in.scope: proposed DEPENDS_ON: the safety case's claim that approximate equilibria of the debate game imply a bounded error rate, in a sketch written with prover-estimator debate in mind

open_obligations: Check whether the paper proves convergence of any training procedure or only correctness at (approximate) Stackelberg equilibria.
Verify that the Stackelberg setting (one debater leads) matches the simultaneous self-play Irving et al. had in mind.
Check that rho-stability and A-provability are plausible for the questions of interest.
out.other_title: Does self-play training stably converge to honest debate equilibria?
out.rationale: Irving et al. note no theory says self-play stably converges to optimal play. Brown-Cohen et al. state that prover-estimator debaters can be trained with standard methods that converge to Stackelberg equilibria, and Theorem 6.2 gives correct answers with probability at least 1 - 5 eps at A-leading Stackelberg equilibria under rho-stability and A-provability; this characterises equilibria rather than proving that gradient training converges.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether standard training can be expected to reach debate equilibria that give correct answers, in complexity-theoretic recursive debate with stable decompositions

text: The authors state that their two main theorems mean debaters can be trained in the prover-estimator debate protocol via standard methods that converge to Stackelberg equilibria in zero-sum games: if claims are rho-stable and the AI debaters only make claims they actually know the answer to (A-provability), Theorem 6.2 implies A will produce the correct answer with probability at least 1-5 eps. If such decompositions are impossible, the soundness case of Theorem 6.1 implies A's payoff will fall below a known threshold, so training success can be read off A's expected payoff.
title: Theorem 6.2: correct answers at Stackelberg equilibria (prob. 1 - 5 eps)
